results.result: VTNg lesions successfully targeted the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden without damaging adjacent structures. Histological assessment confirmed clear loss of large, distinctive cells in the VTNg, with minimal collateral damage to the reticular pontine nucleus (unilateral and contralateral to needle insertion) and restricted loss in the dorsal median raphe adjacent to VTNg. Critically, the lesions did not extend into Gudden's dorsal tegmental nuclei or laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, and acetylcholinesterase staining confirmed intact cholinergic projections from the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus to the anteroventral thalamic nucleus and interpeduncular nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C39 provide converging histological evidence that VTNg lesions were selective and complete. The use of multiple staining methods (Nissl and acetylcholinesterase), quantitative measurements of cholinergic innervation (gray values showing no significant differences from Sham), and systematic assessment of adjacent structures provide strong support for lesion specificity. The minimal collateral damage is well-characterized and unlikely to confound results.

results.result: PCFx lesions produced mammillary body shrinkage consistent with complete postcommissural fornix disconnection. The mean mammillary body area in PCFx animals (1.34 mm²) was significantly smaller than Sham (1.79 mm²; p<0.001) and comparable to previous studies with confirmed disconnection. Cell packing density was significantly increased in PCFx (4054.7 cells/mm²) compared to all other groups (p<0.01), indicating white matter loss without neuronal loss. In contrast, MTTx (1.38 mm²) and VTNx (1.50 mm²) groups showed reduced mammillary body area without increased cell packing, suggesting some neuronal loss in these groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C55 provide quantitative morphometric evidence for lesion effects. The PCFx results are validated by comparison with previous tracer studies (C42-C43), and the increased cell packing provides mechanistic insight into white matter vs. neuronal loss. However, the authors acknowledge the cell counts are not stereological (C56), limiting absolute quantification. The pattern of results across groups is internally consistent and supports the interpretation of differential lesion mechanisms.

results.result: T-maze alternation revealed differential impairments across lesion groups and task stages. In Stage 1 (single maze), only VTNx showed impairment (p=0.005 vs. Sham). In Stage 2 (two mazes, removing intra-maze cues), both MTTx (p=0.004) and VTNx (p=0.006) were impaired relative to Sham, suggesting MTTx animals had masked deficits in Stage 1 by using intra-maze cues. In Stage 3 (darkness, removing visual allocentric cues), both MTTx and VTNx remained impaired relative to both Sham (p<0.025) and PCFx (p<0.03). PCFx animals showed no impairment at any stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C79 present a coherent pattern of behavioral results with appropriate statistical analyses (ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons). The progressive restriction of available cues across stages provides mechanistic insight into the strategies used by different groups. The interpretation that MTTx animals used intra-maze cues in Stage 1 (C68, C142) is well-supported by the emergence of deficits in Stage 2. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=7-8 per group) and statistical corrections are appropriate.

results.result: Radial-arm maze testing revealed spatial working memory deficits in MTTx and VTNx groups. During acquisition (Stage 1), both MTTx and VTNx showed significantly more errors and fewer correct entries in the first 8 choices compared to Sham (p<0.007), with all groups improving across blocks. After maze rotation (Stage 2), which disrupted intra-maze cues, MTTx and VTNx remained impaired relative to Sham (p<0.023), and both differed significantly from PCFx (p<0.03 for errors, p<0.02 for entries). PCFx animals performed comparably to Sham throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C94 provide converging evidence with the T-maze results, showing consistent impairments in MTTx and VTNx but not PCFx. The maze rotation manipulation (Stage 2) effectively tests reliance on allocentric vs. intra-maze cues. Statistical analyses are appropriate with both error and correct entry measures analyzed. The lack of group × block interactions suggests stable group differences rather than learning rate differences. Results support the interpretation that MTTx and VTNx animals are impaired in using allocentric spatial cues.

results.result: All groups successfully acquired the geometric discrimination task at equivalent rates. There were no group differences in escape latency during pre-training (p>0.2) or acquisition (p>0.05), with all groups showing significant improvement across training blocks (p<0.001). During the probe test, all groups spent significantly more time in geometrically correct corners (p<0.001) with no group differences (p>0.05) or group × corner interaction (p>0.05). Swim velocities did not differ between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C104 demonstrate task-specific sparing in MTTx and VTNx groups, providing important evidence that their spatial memory deficits are selective rather than due to non-specific factors like motivation or motor impairment. The geometric discrimination task may rely on different neural systems (head-direction network via lateral mammillary bodies, as suggested by C178-C180). Statistical analyses are appropriate and the probe test provides strong evidence for learning. This dissociation strengthens the interpretation of the T-maze and radial-arm maze deficits.

results.result: MTTx and VTNx lesions produced significant reductions in c-Fos expression in the retrosplenial cortex. Both MTTx (p<0.001) and VTNx (p=0.006) groups had significantly fewer Fos-positive cells than Sham. Critically, PCFx animals had significantly more Fos-positive cells than both MTTx (p=0.001) and VTNx (p=0.026), indicating that PCFx lesions did not produce the hypoactivity seen with MTTx and VTNx lesions.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 provide clear evidence for differential effects of lesions on retrosplenial cortex activity. The c-Fos methodology is appropriate for assessing neural activity, and the 90-minute post-task interval is justified by prior literature (C194). The pattern of results—hypoactivity in MTTx and VTNx but not PCFx—parallels the behavioral findings and supports the interpretation that VTNg inputs, not hippocampal inputs, are critical for maintaining activity in this memory network. Statistical analyses are appropriate with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: MTTx and VTNx lesions reduced hippocampal c-Fos expression, with effects primarily in CA1. Overall hippocampal counts showed a main group effect (p=0.05), with both MTTx (p=0.029) and VTNx (p=0.009) significantly lower than Sham. Subfield analysis revealed significant group differences only in CA1 (p<0.005), with both MTTx and VTNx lower than Sham (p<0.005), but not in dentate gyrus or CA3 (p>0.4).
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C119 demonstrate anatomically specific effects within the hippocampus. The CA1-specific reduction is notable given that MTTx and VTNx lesions do not directly de-afferent the hippocampus (C150), suggesting indirect network effects. The subfield analysis strengthens the findings by showing regional specificity. However, the overall hippocampal effect has a marginal p-value (p=0.05), and the authors acknowledge these are not stereological counts. The pattern is consistent with the retrosplenial cortex findings.

results.result: MTTx and VTNx lesions selectively reduced c-Fos expression in prelimbic cortex but not infralimbic cortex. Prelimbic cortex showed a significant group effect (p=0.006), with both MTTx (p=0.041) and VTNx (p=0.017) lower than Sham. In contrast, infralimbic cortex showed no group differences (p>0.3).
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 demonstrate regional specificity within prefrontal cortex, with prelimbic but not infralimbic involvement. This anatomical specificity strengthens the interpretation that the c-Fos changes reflect disruption of specific memory-related circuits rather than general arousal or activity changes. The dissociation between adjacent cortical regions argues against non-specific effects. Statistical analyses are appropriate.

results.result: No group differences in c-Fos expression were observed in control regions including somatosensory cortex, supramammillary nucleus, lateral septum, or medial septum (all F<1).
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 provide important negative controls demonstrating specificity of the c-Fos effects. The lack of changes in somatosensory cortex argues against non-specific sensorimotor effects. Critically, the lack of changes in supramammillary and septal nuclei (C174) provides evidence against alternative explanations for VTNx effects via these routes, supporting the interpretation that VTNx effects are mediated primarily through mammillary bodies. These negative results strengthen the overall conclusions.

results.result: The study demonstrates that mammillary body function in spatial working memory depends critically on inputs from Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus rather than hippocampal inputs via the postcommissural fornix. Only MTTx and VTNx lesions impaired spatial working memory tasks and disrupted use of allocentric spatial cues, while PCFx lesions produced no behavioral impairments despite causing mammillary body shrinkage equivalent to complete fornix lesions. This pattern was paralleled by c-Fos expression, with MTTx and VTNx but not PCFx producing widespread hypoactivity in memory-related brain regions.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple behavioral tasks (T-maze, radial-arm maze) and c-Fos expression across multiple brain regions. The critical comparison between PCFx (which disconnects hippocampal inputs) and VTNx (which disrupts tegmental inputs) provides strong evidence for the relative importance of these pathways. The validation of PCFx lesions through comparison with previous tracer studies (C42-C43, C146) strengthens confidence in the lesion specificity. However, some alternative explanations remain: (1) the tasks may not sufficiently tax the hippocampal-MB pathway (C157-C158), (2) redundancy via direct hippocampal-thalamic projections may compensate (C159-C162), and (3) VTNx lesions could potentially act through alternative projection sites (C171-C173), though the lack of septal/supramammillary c-Fos changes argues against this (C174).

results.result: Traditional anatomical models of mammillary body function have emphasized hippocampal inputs via the postcommissural fornix, viewing mammillary bodies primarily as a relay of hippocampal information to anterior thalamic nuclei and beyond to cingulate and prefrontal cortices. These models have downplayed other mammillary body afferents and provided no real functional role for the mammillary bodies themselves.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C14 and C128-C131 accurately characterize the historical perspective in the field, supported by appropriate citations to foundational work (Papez, Barbizet, Delay and Brion, Aggleton and Brown). This framing provides essential context for the study's challenge to the dominant model. The characterization of these models' shortcomings (C13-C14) is a reasonable inference that motivates the experimental design. This is primarily a literature review/framing result rather than an empirical finding.

results.result: Anatomical evidence indicates that mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei, with the ventral tegmental nucleus projecting to the medial mammillary nucleus and the dorsal tegmental nucleus projecting to the lateral mammillary nucleus. Previous clinical and behavioral evidence highlights the particular importance of the medial mammillary nucleus for memory, including its consistent atrophy in Korsakoff's syndrome, while the lateral mammillary nucleus is part of the head-direction network.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C21 and C132-C139 provide well-established anatomical background supported by appropriate citations. The distinction between medial and lateral mammillary systems and their differential functions is important for understanding the rationale for targeting VTNg rather than dorsal tegmental nucleus. The clinical evidence from Korsakoff's syndrome (C139) provides translational relevance. This anatomical and clinical background appropriately motivates the experimental focus on VTNg and medial mammillary nucleus.

results.result: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta, and theta-related cells in medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function. VTNg has also been linked to vigilance states and might modulate hippocampal activity. While VTNg innervates other sites (lateral hypothalamus, preoptic area, medial septum, reticular pontine nucleus, median raphe, supramammillary nucleus, ventral tegmental area), these projections appear light and lesions of these alternative sites rarely produce the spatial memory impairments seen with VTNg lesions. The lack of c-Fos changes in supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides evidence that effects are not via these routes.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C175 address the important question of whether VTNx effects are mediated through mammillary bodies or alternative projection sites. The electrophysiological evidence (C166-C167) provides mechanistic insight into how VTNg might influence memory. The discussion of alternative pathways is appropriately cautious, acknowledging uncertainty (C170) while providing evidence against major contributions from alternative routes (C173-C175). The c-Fos evidence from supramammillary and septal nuclei (C174) is particularly valuable for ruling out these alternatives. However, the possibility of contributions from other VTNg targets cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The selectivity of MTTx and VTNx effects for spatial working memory, with sparing of geometric discrimination, suggests effects are not due to non-specific factors like arousal or motivation. The geometric discrimination task may be particularly sensitive to the head-direction system, and MTT lesions likely disconnect medial but not lateral mammillary body efferents, providing support for dissociation of two memory systems within the mammillary bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C180 provide important interpretation of the dissociation between impaired spatial working memory and intact geometric discrimination. The inference about task-specific neural systems is supported by citations (C178) and anatomical reasoning (C179). This dissociation strengthens the argument against non-specific effects and supports the existence of parallel memory systems within mammillary bodies. However, the interpretation relies on assumptions about which mammillary body subdivisions are affected by MTT lesions that are not directly verified in this study.

results.result: Clinical studies show that mammillary bodies and mammillothalamic tract are important for human memory, particularly recollective memory. The situation regarding human VTNg is less clear—its existence in humans was historically doubted, though it is now apparent that VTNg structure and connections are remarkably similar across species. Only one amnesic patient with restricted VTN damage has been reported, with limited imaging available.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C186 appropriately discuss translational relevance and limitations. The clinical evidence for mammillary body and MTT importance in humans (C181-C182) is well-established and properly cited. The discussion of VTNg in humans (C183-C186) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging the limited clinical evidence while noting cross-species anatomical conservation. This honest assessment of translational limitations is appropriate and does not undermine the rat findings.

results.result: The pattern of behavioral impairments was paralleled by c-Fos findings, with both VTNx and MTTx producing significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells in hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex. These changes reflect 'indirect' effects since MTT and VTNg lesions do not directly de-afferent these sites. Reduced activity in memory-related networks appears to be a consistent marker of medial diencephalic damage in animals and humans, though whether this contributes to deficits or is merely symptomatic remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 appropriately synthesize the c-Fos findings and place them in broader context. The parallel between behavioral and c-Fos patterns strengthens both sets of findings. The distinction between direct and indirect effects (C150) is important for interpretation. The discussion of whether hypoactivity is causal or symptomatic (C151-C153) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging uncertainty while citing relevant evidence from antisense studies. This measured interpretation is appropriate given the correlational nature of c-Fos data.

results.result: The lack of PCFx effects is surprising and raises questions about the function of the hippocampal-mammillary body pathway. Possible explanations include: (1) the tasks may not have sufficiently taxed this pathway, (2) redundancy with direct hippocampal-thalamic projections may compensate for PCFx lesions, though it is unclear whether these pathways convey the same information since they arise from different cell populations. Some studies show fornix lesions more disruptive than MB lesions (consistent with supportive direct hippocampal-thalamic inputs), while others show the opposite pattern, highlighting potential importance of additional information streams from limbic midbrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C164 provide thoughtful discussion of alternative explanations for the surprising lack of PCFx effects. The comparison with previous PCFx studies (C154-C155) validates the current lesions. The discussion of potential explanations (C157-C164) is appropriately speculative, acknowledging uncertainty while considering multiple possibilities supported by literature. The acknowledgment that the tasks may not optimally test the hippocampal-MB pathway (C157-C158) is an important limitation. The discussion of redundancy and parallel pathways (C159-C164) provides a plausible framework for understanding the results without overinterpreting them.

results.result: MTTx and VTNx lesions impaired spatial working memory tasks (T-maze alternation and radial-arm maze), particularly disrupting the use of extramaze spatial landmarks, while PCFx lesions produced no impairment. The MTTx and VTNx groups performed equivalently to each other but significantly worse than Sham and PCFx groups, suggesting these lesion groups were less able to use allocentric cues and more reliant on intra-maze cues.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings as 'interesting and important results' and describe them as 'remarkable,' particularly noting the maze rotation effects that dissociate extramaze from intramaze cue use. The reviewers accept the behavioral dissociation between PCFx lesions (no effect) and MTTx/VTNx lesions (impaired performance), treating this as a key finding of the study.

results.result: All lesion groups (MTTx, VTNx, PCFx) were able to learn the geometric discrimination task at the same rate and level as Sham controls, with no group differences in acquisition or probe performance. This sparing of geometric discrimination performance, despite MTTx lesions likely disconnecting medial MB efferents while leaving lateral MB efferents intact, supports the dissociation of two memory systems within the mammillary bodies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings and implicitly accept them as part of the overall pattern of results. The lack of impairment on geometric discrimination is treated as consistent with the selectivity of the spatial memory deficits and the dissociation of memory systems within the mammillary bodies.

results.result: MTTx and VTNx lesions produced widespread reductions in c-Fos expression in memory-related regions including retrosplenial cortex, hippocampus (particularly CA1), and prelimbic cortex, while PCFx lesions did not produce these widespread reductions. The pattern of c-Fos findings paralleled the behavioral impairments, with both VTNx and MTTx groups showing significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells in these regions compared to Sham and PCFx groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the c-Fos findings but express concern that 'the situation is likely to be rather complicated and other pathways could also be directly or indirectly involved.' They also request more detailed analysis, specifically asking about 'which neurons and layer are or are not c-Fos positive' in the hippocampus, indicating the evidence is incomplete or insufficiently characterized.

results.result: VTNg lesions produced clear loss of large distinctive cells in the ventral tegmental nucleus, with very limited collateral damage to adjacent structures. The laterodorsal tegmental nuclei and their cholinergic projections remained intact, as confirmed by acetylcholinesterase staining showing no significant differences between VTNx and Sham groups in the anteroventral thalamic nucleus or interpeduncular nucleus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the lesions as 'very precise' and do not question the histological characterization of the VTNg lesions or the assessment of collateral damage. The specificity of the lesions is implicitly accepted as adequate for the study's conclusions.

results.result: PCFx lesions produced significant mammillary body shrinkage (mean area 1.34 mm² vs 1.79 mm² in Sham, p<0.001) equivalent to complete fornix lesions, with increased cell packing in the PCFx group indicating loss of white matter rather than neuronal loss. MTTx and VTNx lesions also reduced mammillary body size, but without increased cell packing, suggesting some cell loss in these groups. The PCFx lesions were indistinguishable from those previously demonstrated to completely disconnect hippocampal formation-MB projections.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express concern that 'it is difficult to determine this from Figure 1G,H' and request 'improved photomicrographs' and potentially 'measurements of the neurons' to substantiate the conclusion about white matter loss versus neuronal loss. They also ask whether 'MMT or VTNg lesions have no effect on MB neurons' and whether 'there are changes in the expression of c-Fos in the different MB subdivisions,' indicating the anatomical characterization is incomplete.

results.result: The findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function dominated by hippocampal inputs. Instead, the results suggest that the more crucial inputs for MB spatial function are from VTNg rather than the hippocampal formation, supporting a novel model of limbic brain interactions where the MBs have important roles in memory that can be independent of their hippocampal inputs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly request 'more detailed, explicit discussion of their ideas' about the role of the PCF, noting that 'the lack of effect of PCFx lesions can be considered surprising' in classical views. They ask 'What then is the role of the PCF?' indicating the authors need to provide clearer interpretation and consider alternative explanations such as whether 'the tasks used in the present study did not sufficiently tax this pathway.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on VTNg lesion specificity and histological characterization (C29-C39). Both evaluations find the evidence for selective and complete lesions with minimal collateral damage to be well-supported. Reviewers describe lesions as 'very precise' while OpenEval notes 'strong support for lesion specificity.'

Disagreement on PCFx morphometric evidence (C40-C55). OpenEval finds the quantitative evidence supported despite acknowledged limitations in stereology. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, stating 'it is difficult to determine this from Figure 1G,H' and request improved photomicrographs and additional measurements, indicating the anatomical characterization is incomplete.

Agreement on T-maze behavioral findings (C58-C79). Both evaluations accept the behavioral results showing MTTx/VTNx impairments with appropriate statistical analyses. Peer reviewers describe findings as 'interesting and important results' and 'remarkable,' particularly the maze rotation effects. OpenEval notes coherent pattern with progressive cue restriction providing mechanistic insight.

Agreement on radial-arm maze results (C80-C94). Both evaluations support the convergence with T-maze findings showing consistent MTTx/VTNx impairments. Peer reviewers accept the behavioral dissociation between PCFx (no effect) and MTTx/VTNx lesions as a key finding. OpenEval emphasizes the maze rotation manipulation effectively tests allocentric versus intra-maze cue reliance.

Agreement on geometric discrimination task sparing (C95-C104). Both evaluations accept the intact performance in MTTx/VTNx groups. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as consistent with selectivity of spatial memory deficits. OpenEval emphasizes this dissociation as important evidence against non-specific factors and supports parallel memory systems within mammillary bodies (C176-C180).

Partial disagreement on retrosplenial cortex c-Fos findings (C107-C111). OpenEval finds clear evidence for differential effects with appropriate methodology. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but express uncertainty, noting 'the situation is likely to be rather complicated and other pathways could also be directly or indirectly involved,' indicating concerns about interpretation complexity.

Disagreement on hippocampal c-Fos findings (C112-C119). OpenEval supports the CA1-specific reduction despite marginal p-value and acknowledges non-stereological limitations. Peer reviewers request more detailed analysis, specifically asking 'which neurons and layer are or are not c-Fos positive,' indicating the evidence is incomplete or insufficiently characterized.

Partial disagreement on prefrontal cortex c-Fos findings (C120-C123). OpenEval supports the prelimbic/infralimbic dissociation as evidence of anatomical specificity. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but express general concern about c-Fos interpretation complexity and request more detailed characterization across brain regions.

Partial agreement on negative control c-Fos findings (C124-C127). OpenEval emphasizes these as important evidence for specificity, particularly lack of supramammillary/septal changes. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge these findings but their request for more detailed c-Fos analysis suggests they want additional characterization to strengthen conclusions.

Agreement on main conclusion about VTNg versus hippocampal inputs (C3-C7, C140-C145, C165, C188). Both evaluations support the overarching finding that VTNg inputs are more critical than hippocampal inputs for spatial memory. Peer reviewers describe the behavioral dissociation as 'interesting and important.' OpenEval notes converging evidence while acknowledging alternative explanations remain.

Agreement on need for better explanation of PCFx results (C154-C164, C156-C159, C187). Both evaluations recognize the surprising lack of PCFx effects requires interpretation. Peer reviewers explicitly request 'more detailed, explicit discussion' and ask 'What then is the role of the PCF?' OpenEval finds the discussion appropriately speculative but acknowledges tasks may not optimally test the hippocampal-MB pathway.

OpenEval evaluates anatomical background on medial/lateral mammillary systems (C15-C21, C132-C139) as well-supported with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this anatomical context.

OpenEval evaluates discussion of VTNx mechanisms and alternative pathways (C166-C175) as supported, noting c-Fos evidence from supramammillary/septal nuclei helps rule out alternatives. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers' general concern about pathway complexity may relate to these claims.

Agreement on interpretation of geometric discrimination dissociation (C176-C180). OpenEval supports the inference about task-specific neural systems and parallel memory pathways. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this interpretation as consistent with the overall pattern, treating the dissociation as evidence for selectivity.

OpenEval evaluates translational relevance discussion (C181-C186) as appropriately cautious about human VTNg evidence while noting cross-species conservation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this translational discussion.

Partial disagreement on synthesis of c-Fos findings (C147-C153). OpenEval finds the synthesis appropriate with measured interpretation of causal versus symptomatic relationships. Peer reviewers' request for more detailed c-Fos analysis and concern about pathway complexity suggests they find the synthesis incomplete or requiring additional support.
